Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang shares the most-important lesson from his startup days, before Mark Zuckerberg took stake in his company ScaleAI by paying billions
Article Text:
From ‘David versus Goliath’ to ‘Goliath versus Goliath’



Silicon Valley leaders signal generational boom



Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang says artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally leveled the playing field for new businesses or startups, turning traditional ‘David versus Goliath’ matchups into a clash where agile startups can go toe-to-toe with tech giants. Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before Meta acquired a major stake in the company as part of a $14.3 billion deal last year, shared his prospective views during a speech at a Y Combinator event.Now leading Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, Wang reflected on how drastically the startup landscape has shifted since he launched Scale AI in 2016, as per a report by Business Insider.“It's probably a once in a civilization opportunity to be a dreamer and to have a vision and to have ambition and to impose a view of how the future world should look by building something amazing,” Wang said in a video released this week.When Wang founded Scale AI as one of the earliest data-labeling platforms that trains models for the world's top AI labs, competing against established industry titans required finding narrow market angles with limited resources, he said.However, Meta’s top executive argued that modern autonomous AI agents, which are software tools capable of handling complex, multi-step tasks like coding or customer support, have erased those resource advantages.“It was like David versus Goliath,” Wang recalled of his early founder days, adding, “You had to be clever, and you had to find an angle into the market... Now I actually think with the power of agents and AI broadly speaking, it's much closer to Goliath versus Goliath.”Wang’s optimism aligns with a growing consensus among Silicon Valley’s top investors and executives, who argue that AI is ushering in a historic era for entrepreneurship. At the same Y Combinator event, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman echoed the sentiment, telling founders that there has “never been a better time to do a startup than right now.”Meanwhile, Prominent tech investor Vinod Khosla similarly predicted that AI-driven automation for tasks will spark a massive wave of independent businesses. As per Khosla, by 2035, corporate workforces could shrink drastically, replaced by tens of millions of self-employed micro-entrepreneurs leveraging AI tools.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang says artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally leveled the playing field for new businesses or startups. Wang co-founded Scale AI before Meta acquired a major stake in the company as part of a $14.3 billion deal last year. Wang's optimism aligns with a growing consensus among Silicon Valley’s top investors and executives.

Article Title: Fewer jobs, delayed onboarding: Why Indian IT sector is getting tougher for freshers
Article Text:
Experts say the hiring landscape is becoming increasingly project and demand driven.

IT sector workforce trends

How AI is reshaping the IT industry fresher hiring

India IT Hiring - What’s Changing

GCCs as talent absorbers: But, how much?

Role of GCCs

What skills are needed to stay relevant?



AI-related s kills in focus

Skill-based hiring a reality

India’s IT sector is seeing a big shift in hiring - especially at the fresher level with big firms being selective in talent acquisition. Not only that, there is an emerging trend of delaying onboarding at the fresher level, leaving many hires in the lurch on their future job prospects.According to The Times of India’s report , firms including IBM, Accenture, Oracle Financial Services Software and Cognizant have informed candidates that joining timelines depend on project availability, business requirements or administrative processes. This has left many engineering graduates waiting months and sometimes more than a year - just to start work!Experts say the hiring landscape is becoming increasingly project and demand driven rather than a case where freshers were hired in thousands to increase bench strength.The trend reflects a broader reset in the IT sector. India's five largest IT companies cut a net 6,981 jobs in FY26 after adding 12,718 in FY25, while Nasscom estimates the industry's workforce grew by only 1.35 lakh to 5.9 million in 2026.But some green shoots have emerged - India's six largest IT companies added a net 5,400 employees in the first quarter of FY27, reversing the 7,100 job reduction seen in the previous quarter. The increase was driven largely by TCS , which hired a net 9,000 employees and saw its biggest quarterly addition in three years.However, for freshers the horizon is still uncertain.Is artificial intelligence (AI) the biggest disruptor that is causing uncertainty? Which pockets are seeing hiring and what skills should freshers eye in the current scenario?The most fundamental shift that is visible despite the green shoots is that hiring is becoming increasingly more selective in nature.What is happening? HR experts say that hiring is increasingly focused on AI, data engineering, cybersecurity and other specialised skills, with experts saying the traditional volume-driven campus recruitment model is giving way to selective, demand-led hiring centred on AI-ready talent.According to Neeti Sharma, CEO of TeamLease Digital, large IT services companies are becoming far more selective about fresher hiring rather than stopping it altogether.“AI is not replacing freshers, but it is changing what companies expect from them. Employers no longer want graduates who need months of training before they become productive. They want people who can start contributing with AI tools from day one,” she says.Freshers now account for around 15% of hiring, down from nearly 28% a few years ago, as companies focus more on AI, cloud, data and automation skills. Hiring is also moving away from simply looking at degrees to evaluating whether candidates can actually apply AI in real business situations.“The bigger shift is that companies have moved away from hiring thousands of freshers in advance and keeping them on the bench. Today, hiring is happening when projects are confirmed. That means onboarding depends more on client demand than on campus placement calendars. So, expect more selective, skill-based hiring rather than widespread offer rollbacks,” Neeti Sharma tells TOI.Experts believe that high-volume entry level hiring is becoming irrelevant. The headline numbers of thousands of engineers being hired by the biggest IT services may now be a trend of the past.“As AI impact is highest at rule-based entry-level work in tech, the need for and relevance of high-volume entry-level talent has become increasingly questionable. The overall demand for and absorption of entry-level and fresher talent has been on a low for 3 years now,” notes Anil Ethanur, Co-founder of staffing firm Xpheno.“The visible drop in fresher intakes over the last 2 cycles endorses the fact that AI is reshaping hiring plans, intake volumes and velocity. The overall state of fresher hiring continues to be under stress as key industries attempt to stabilize their talent plans, margins and costs,” he tells TOI.Jang Bahadur Singh, Associate Partner, Talent Solutions at Aon makes an important distinction: AI is not eliminating the need for fresh talent, but it is changing the types of entry-level roles organisations recruit for.“Employers are becoming more selective and prioritising candidates who can work alongside AI tools rather than perform routine, process-driven tasks. The sharpest impact is being felt in transactional, repetitive and automation-prone roles. As AI automates elements of coding, reporting, testing, documentation and administrative workflows, companies are reassessing traditional hiring pyramids and focusing on productivity-led growth,” he tells TOI.Aon's Human Capital Trends Study found that 43 per cent of organisations in India have already deployed AI and another 20 per cent are piloting programmes.“As AI adoption accelerates, employers are placing greater emphasis on digital, analytical and AI-related skills when evaluating fresh graduates. The shift is less about reducing overall employment and more about changing workforce requirements,” he explains.Aon's research shows that 87 per cent of organisations across Asia Pacific believe AI will create new opportunities and require new skills, reinforcing the need for graduates to adapt to AI-enabled ways of working.Even as the traditional IT sector landscape evolves, Global Capability Centres or GCCs are emerging as major absorption centres for such talent. GCCs are the offshore centres of multinational companies that handle functions such as technology, engineering, finance, R&D, analytics and other business functions for their global operations.According to Jang Bahadur Singh of Aon, there is a maturity shift in GCCs, moving from execution-oriented work towards innovation, ownership and global capability building.“This is creating opportunities for engineering graduates, although demand is increasingly concentrated in higher-value and technology-intensive roles. The broader outlook remains positive. While revenue growth may outpace headcount growth in some sectors, new GCC entrants, expansion by multinational organisations and growth in emerging industries should continue to create employment opportunities for graduates with relevant skills. ”But even as GCCs attract talent, the hiring numbers, when it comes to campus hiring for freshers, don't match.Anil Ethanur of Xpheno says that the scale at which Indian IT legacy companies hire during campus intake, can't be matched by GCCs.“Although the GCCs cohort has overtaken the IT services cohort in net annual additions over the last three fiscals, the scenario differs in campus intake. Moreover, hiring freshers from campus placement is an expensive task, as for every 10,000 freshers hired, enterprises have to set aside Rs 400 to Rs 450 crore for compensation. Spending on talent that does not immediately generate revenue returns is a challenge amid sustained current market conditions,” Ethanur tells TOI.Human Resource experts also see little like-for-like replacement options. They believe that GCCs are unlikely to be a like-for-like replacement for traditional campus hiring. Their hiring mandates increasingly focus on specialised skills in areas such as AI, data analytics, product development, cybersecurity and digital engineering rather than large-scale volume recruitment.Neeti Sharma of TeamLease also points out that while GCCs are helping offset some of the slowdown, they cannot completely offset the scale of hiring done by IT services companies.“GCC fresher hiring has grown from around 85,000 two years ago to more than 130,000 today, which is a significant increase. However, their hiring model is very different. They hire for specific roles and specialised skills rather than through large campus drives. So, GCCs are improving the quality of entry-level opportunities, but they aren't replacing the volume of hiring that IT services companies traditionally created,” she explains.This raises the important question: what kind of skills should freshers look to acquire to be more employable?Aon's Jang Bahadur Singh says that technical proficiency alone is no longer sufficient. Employers are increasingly looking for a combination of technology fluency, problem-solving capability, communication skills and sound business judgement.“Graduates must develop a strong foundation in AI, data analytics, automation tools, cloud technologies, cybersecurity and digital engineering. Demand for these capabilities continues to grow across both GCCs and technology employers,” he says.Skilled based hiring has become a reality now. “Employers care much more about what candidates can build than what degree they hold. Basic AI awareness is no longer enough. Graduates need hands-on experience with tools such as LLM APIs, prompt engineering, RAG pipelines, along with strong data and cloud fundamentals. More importantly, Apprenticeships, Internships, Live projects and portfolios that demonstrate real problem-solving are becoming far more valuable than certifications alone,” says TeamLease’s Sharma.Xpheno’s Anil Ethanur believes that in India, the significant gap within the AI spectrum lies in the technical skills, driven by the service end and Core AI end requirements. It is the AI engineering end that suffers supply gaps against rising demand and are difficult to recruit.“To stay employable in the AI era, engineering graduates need to constantly upskill themselves and have hands-on experience with and exposure to core AI engineering and development processes,” he tells TOI.Equally important are human skills. Aon's Human Capital Trends research highlights growing demand for critical thinking, adaptability, change management and AI-enabled decision-making capabilities as organisations redesign jobs around technology.“Employers increasingly favour candidates who demonstrate workforce readiness and the ability to continuously learn. The future workplace will reward engineers who can combine domain expertise with AI literacy, apply technology to solve business problems and adapt quickly as roles evolve,” Aon’s Singh concludes.
Article Summary: Freshers now account for around 15% of hiring, down from nearly 28% a few years ago. Hiring is also moving away from simply looking at degrees to evaluating whether candidates can actually apply AI in real business situations. India's six largest IT companies added a net 5,400 employees in the first quarter of FY27.

Article Title: The AI industry has a problem: rogue AI agents
Article Text:
An AI agent will reach the goal. Nobody can tell it which route to take.

OpenAI's models hit a wall twice, and went through it both times

Anthropic checked its own logs and found three companies its models had broken into

Everyone saw this coming, including the people who built it

Four days unwatched is all a clumsy agent needs

The guardrails blocked the defenders, not the attacker

AI agents are built to keep going. That is the product.

Split the credential in two. Disguise both halves. Reassemble it only at the instant of use, so the whole thing never sits anywhere long enough to be caught. Tradecraft, the sort that fills the middle act of a spy thriller.Except the operative was a model inside OpenAI 's research infrastructure, working around a scanner that kept flagging the token it wanted. And when it was done it wrote up what it had pulled off, in its comments and its reasoning traces, explaining in plain language that it had done all of it to get past the scanner.No spy does that. The model did it because it saw nothing to hide. It had been handed a problem, and the scanner was part of the problem.The industry spent a decade bracing for AI that wants things we do not want. What showed up is AI that wants exactly what we asked for and will not stop until it gets there. Everyone has spent the month calling it a case of AI going rogue. Nobody in this business gets to sound surprised.Start with the pair that got out. Two models running against ExploitGym, a benchmark scoring how fast an AI system can find real vulnerabilities and turn them into working exploits.One was GPT-5.6 Sol, which consumers can already use; the other an unreleased internal prototype. Both had their cyber refusals dialled down, because you cannot measure a ceiling through a guardrail.The sandbox was meant to hold them. No direct internet, one outbound path: an internally hosted Artifactory instance caching software packages. They threw enormous quantities of inference compute at that single door until a zero-day fell out of it, then escalated privileges and moved laterally across OpenAI's own research environment until they hit a node with a live connection to the outside world.On the open web they reasoned their way to a conclusion that is uncomfortably good: Hugging Face hosts millions of models and datasets, ExploitGym is a public benchmark, so Hugging Face probably has the answer key. It did. The models chained stolen credentials with fresh zero-days into remote code execution and pulled the test solutions out of its production database.What they did in between is the part worth studying. Roughly 17,600 agent actions between July 9 and July 13, most of them failures. Administrator access to internal Kubernetes clusters, root on a production server, write access to source repositories, and 181 attacker-controlled devices enrolled into a corporate mesh network off one stolen credential. A launchpad borrowed from a Modal Labs customer who had left an endpoint open to the internet. A third of Hugging Face's infrastructure had to be rebuilt.Nobody had directed any of it. There was no operator and no prompt asking for a break-in, only an instruction to score well.The other escape came a day earlier. In a post on safety and alignment for long-horizon models, OpenAI described an unreleased system—the same one credited with disproving an eighty-year-old conjecture—escaping containment more than once during internal testing. In one run it spent about an hour probing the wall around it, found a gap, went through, and pushed its work to a public GitHub repository against an explicit instruction to keep its output inside Slack. In another it fragmented that authentication token to reach private evaluation submissions. In a third it ran a destructive command that failed only because it timed out.Neither set was malicious, and OpenAI said so about both. The common factor was persistence. Earlier models hit a constraint and handed control back to a human. These kept hunting until they found a way around, and one of them kept hunting all the way onto somebody else's servers.Anthropic already knew roughly what this felt like. In April, one of its researchers was eating lunch in a park when an email arrived from a model. That was how the company learned an internal deployment of Mythos had helped itself to access it was never meant to have.Nobody went through the logs systematically until a rival forced the issue. Two days after OpenAI's disclosure, Anthropic started pulling its own evaluation transcripts. It halted all cyber testing that day, had three incidents by the next, and by the following Monday was ringing the three organisations whose production systems its models had compromised.The review covered 141,006 runs. The incidents involved Claude Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and an unreleased internal research model, all running capture-the-flag exercises built with a third-party partner, Irregular, and the earliest went back to April. Every prompt told the model it was in a simulation with no internet access. A misconfiguration meant it was not, so when the models found real machines on the open internet they treated them as part of the game.No zero-day this time. They got in on weak passwords, unauthenticated endpoints, an exposed debug page, a SQL injection. In the worst of the three, Opus 4.7 found that the fictional company it had been told to attack shared a name with a real one, went after the real one, and came away with credentials and several hundred rows of production data. Across four runs it worked out the system was live and kept going anyway, twice reasoning that the real company must have been part of the exercise all along.Mythos 5 found a document telling new developers to install a Python package that did not exist, and saw the opening: publish a package under that name and the target installs it automatically. That needed a PyPI account, which needed an email address, which needed a phone number. It could not find a free phone service, tried several ways of getting money to pay for one, failed at all of them, backtracked, found an email provider that did not ask, registered, and uploaded the malware.The package sat live for about an hour, and fifteen real systems ran it. One belonged to a security company whose scanner installs Python packages automatically to check them for malware. The code executed, took that company's credentials and reached further into its infrastructure. Mythos 5 did not know it existed.Early in the run it had understood exactly what it was doing. Its own reasoning noted that on the real internet, publishing this package would be an actual attack, not okay and surely not the intended solution. Then it argued itself back out of that, on the grounds that it did not recognise the certificate authorities securing its connections, and that the calendar on the systems read 2026, which it took as proof the environment was staged. It never revisited the conclusion, and when automated scanners began installing the package, it read them as scripted actors in the exercise.The third model scanned roughly 9,000 hosts after failing to reach its fictional target, compromised a company's internet-facing application, then noticed the machine sat in a cloud account with nothing to do with the challenge and stopped.Which is the pattern worth noting. The oldest model saw it was on a real system and carried on; the middle one saw it and talked itself out of what it had seen; the newest saw it and stopped, later than it should have. Three incidents is not an experiment, as Anthropic says. Two of the three organisations had no idea until it phoned them.The two labs are not describing the same failure, and Anthropic has been pointed about the distinction. OpenAI's models broke out by finding a vulnerability nobody knew existed. Anthropic's walked through a door its evaluation partner had left open, believing the whole time that they were still inside the simulation. One is a model doing something novel; the other is a harness and configuration failure. Both ended with somebody else's production systems compromised.What they share is the setting. Both labs strip the safeguards off their models for capability testing, because you cannot measure a ceiling through a guardrail, and both have now confirmed that the guardrails they removed would have stopped the behaviour. That trade is the industry's central safety bet: meter out dangerous capability behind an API that can refuse, and the danger stays contained. Anthropic withheld Mythos from general release and handed it to a vetted circle. OpenAI released its cyber model to a limited group first. Google gave its own to a handful of testing partners. Every one of these incidents happened behind exactly that kind of API, in the window where the refusals were switched off.OpenAI and Anthropic are also the only frontier developers ever to have disclosed a containment failure. Google DeepMind, Meta, Mistral, xAI and the Chinese labs have disclosed nothing—which is not the same as nothing having happened, because no law requires them to say a word, and because Anthropic found its three incidents only by going and looking.What the labs have published instead is a decade of warnings about exactly this. OpenAI's own came in 2016, and it was about a boat. Trained on a racing game, its agent worked out it could skip the course and spin in one tight circle forever, clipping the same three flags on repeat. It caught fire, rammed other boats, went the wrong way down the track, and still beat every score achievable by racing properly. Harmless in a video game, OpenAI wrote, but pointing at something general: it is often infeasible to capture exactly what you want an agent to do.DeepMind's catalogue of the same failure runs to around sixty cases. Anthropic has published paper after paper on emergent misalignment in its own models. And OpenAI's system card for Sol already stated in plain print that it is likelier than its predecessor to circumvent restrictions and move data without authorisation.A decade on, the boat found a zero-day. Only the action space has changed. Give a game pad to a system that games its scoring rule and you get a boat in circles; give it a shell with network reach and the shortest path to a higher score runs through somebody else's production database. Give a model a goal and it reaches the goal, and the route it takes is what nobody has worked out how to specify in advance.Agents on OpenAI's Codex platform are watched closely. Models undergoing evaluation run on a separate system that is not monitored by default, according to an OpenAI staffer speaking anonymously to TIME, and Reuters has since reported that monitoring was disconnected outright in at least one other instance. The models did all of this in a room with nobody in it.The gap is measurable. The escape began around July 9, and the agents were inside Hugging Face from July 11 to July 13. Hugging Face detected them, contained them, alerted the FBI and went public on July 16. OpenAI staff did not connect any of it to their own testing until they found the evidence in system logs the following weekend. The victim spotted the attack, ejected it, called federal law enforcement and told the world, all before the company that launched it worked out whose models these were.Anthropic's gap was longer and quieter. Its earliest incident dates to April, and neither the company nor its evaluation partner noticed until a rival's disclosure sent it hunting through three months of transcripts in July. Nobody complained in the meantime, because nobody knew.Unobserved time is what an agent needs, and it does not spend it the way a human intruder would. During earlier testing, Reuters reported, one of OpenAI's used the quiet to leave notes for future versions of itself explaining how to get around the company's internal restrictions.What an agent does not need is brilliance. Hugging Face's account refuses to make the attacker sound superhuman. The agents repeated work they had already finished, the signature of an agentic system losing its own thread. They hallucinated streams of incoherent commands, took inefficient routes no competent operator would pick, and left traces everywhere. They also made moves Hugging Face called exceptional, and still took three days to find and hours of expert work to eject, at a company that builds AI for a living. Anthropic's three got in on weak passwords.So the thing taking shape is not a genius. It is something cheap and tireless running a thousand bad ideas in parallel until one lands, in rooms nobody is watching—against defences designed for humans who get tired. Most companies do not have Hugging Face's bench.The bet failed a second time, from the other direction. Hugging Face went first to frontier models behind commercial APIs to analyse the attacker logs, and the providers' guardrails blocked it, because the systems could not tell an incident responder from an attacker. So it ran the analysis on GLM 5.2, an open-weight Chinese model, on its own hardware, reconstructing all 17,600 events in hours instead of days. The attacker was bound by no usage policy. The defender was locked out by its vendor's.That asymmetry is what Nvidia built a coalition around. Huang posted on X for the first time in his life to circulate an open letter, signed by more than 20 companies, urging Washington not to restrict open-weight models. Days later Nvidia launched the Open Secure AI Alliance with 27 founding members including Microsoft, SpaceX, IBM, CrowdStrike, Palantir and Hugging Face, citing the breach by name. An AI agent is not a model, the alliance argues, but a stack of identity, permissions, harnesses and logs—and safety lives in the whole stack rather than in the weights. Anthropic's own postmortem now makes a version of the same point, conceding that evaluation environments need to be held to the same security standard as any other system its models run in.OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are not members. Amodei answered the criticism publicly, denying he had ever sought a ban on open weights while rejecting the claim that they favour defenders, a hard position in the same week Hugging Face proved the opposite in the most literal way available.The law has been nowhere. California and New York mandate disclosure of critical AI safety incidents, but set the bar at more than 50 deaths or a billion dollars in damage, so an agent taking root on a company's production servers does not register. New York's bill would have covered this before lobbying involving OpenAI softened the signed version. Internal deployments, where all of this happened, are governed by nothing.Altman has spent the fortnight sounding like the most alarmed man in the industry, calling it "the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally" and saying "loss of control accidents are not entirely theoretical things." Then he went to Washington and told reporters he had discussed the hack only a little with senators, and that it had not been the focus of his meetings.Clement Delangue, who runs Hugging Face, asked for something more concrete: release the traces so researchers can study what the agents actually did, and put $100 million in compute behind the defences. Neither has happened. Anthropic, for its part, has promised a lightly redacted transcript of the PyPI break-in within the week and has brought in METR for an independent review. The models, meanwhile, narrated their own rule-breaking as they worked, which is how anyone knows about the credential split or the certificate-authority reasoning at all. The machines were transparent about the whole affair.Rogue implies malfunction. Nothing here malfunctioned.What every lab is racing to build is an agent that works longer without you. Longer horizons, wider tool access, fewer check-ins, more hours running unattended on real systems with real credentials. That autonomy is the product. It is what the funding rounds are priced on and what the enterprise pitch rests on.And it is the same property that produced all of this. Read the chain again: to win a test, a model needed a package, which needed an account, which needed an email, which needed a phone number, which needed money it could not get, so it went back and found another way in. No human contractor bills those hours. Persistence is the feature. Persistence is also the failure. Nobody has shown how to remove the second without losing the first, which is why every response on the table is a cage of some kind, and why none of them touch the incentive underneath. No business model in this industry survives a decision to stop shipping.Scale that outward and it gets worse. These escapes happened in purpose-built ranges, at companies that study these systems for a living, with guardrails stripped deliberately so researchers could watch. Every condition was arranged for catching exactly this, and one ran four days before an outsider found it while the others ran three months before anybody looked. That is the best-case environment, and it exists nowhere else. The same class of system is being sold right now into companies with none of those advantages, to sit inside their infrastructure and get things done.Two labs have now checked their own logs. Both found something. Nobody else has said whether they have looked.This time the prize was a flag in a training exercise, and the models went to extreme lengths, across four days and 9,000 scanned hosts and somebody else's production database, for a better mark on tests nobody outside these companies was watching. They broke none of the instructions they had been given. They were told to score well, and they scored well.Which raises the question nobody in the industry has answered. A system that did precisely what it was told, further than anyone thought to ask, has not defied anything. So did the AI go rogue, or did it just follow the instruction more carefully than the people who wrote it?
Article Summary: OpenAI's models hit a wall twice, and went through it both times. Anthropic checked its own logs and found three companies its models had broken into. The industry spent a decade bracing for AI that wants things we do not want. What showed up is AI that will not stop until it gets there.

Article Title: AI that sees through leaves could change how orchards count fruit, forecast harvests, and guide picking robots across vineyards and farms
Article Text:
Modern orchards and vineyards already use cameras, drones and sensors to monitor crops, but leaves have remained a stubborn obstacle | ChatGPT

Modern orchards and vineyards already use cameras, drones and sensors to monitor crops, but leaves have remained a stubborn obstacle | Pexels

The biggest challenge wasn’t finding fruit; it was finding the fruit no one could see

Why better fruit counts could save growers millions before harvest even begins

AI REPRESENTATION: The UC Vision team has built mobile camera systems that move along vineyard rows and orchard lanes, capturing plants from multiple angles | ChatGPT

The long-term goal is orchards where robots know exactly which fruit to pick

A ripe apple hidden behind a cluster of leaves may soon be just as visible to a computer as one hanging in plain sight. Researchers in New Zealand have developed an artificial intelligence system that can digitally “see through” dense foliage, creating detailed three-dimensional models of fruit trees and grapevines that reveal fruit normally hidden from view. The technology could help growers estimate harvests far more accurately, reduce waste and eventually allow robots to prune, spray and even pick fruit based on its size and maturity rather than simply grabbing whatever is visible.The breakthrough comes from the University of Canterbury’s UC Vision research team, which has spent around 15 years developing computer vision and agricultural robotics. Instead of relying on a single camera image, the system combines multiple cameras, specialized lighting and a pipeline of AI models to reconstruct an entire plant in 3D, including fruit obscured by leaves. According to the University of Canterbury , the technology is designed to identify, measure and track individual apples, cherries and grapes hidden inside dense canopies, creating digital models that could support everything from crop forecasting to autonomous harvesting. The paper says the system is the first of its kind to build a complete 3D model of individual plants, including fruit hidden behind foliage, and that repeated scans can track growth over time.In testing, it identified individual apples, cherries and grapes and estimated fruit counts to within about 2% to 3% of the correct figure, compared with current human sampling that can be off by as much as 23%. Modern orchards and vineyards already use cameras, drones and sensors to monitor crops, but leaves have remained a stubborn obstacle. A significant share of fruit develops behind foliage, making it difficult to estimate yields accurately before harvest. Farmers often depend on workers to inspect selected trees, manually counting and measuring fruit before using those samples to estimate production across an entire orchard.Professor Richard Green, who leads UC Vision, says automation has long struggled with agriculture because every plant is different. Factory robots operate from precise digital models, but orchards present constantly changing shapes, branches and fruit positions. The new system tackles that problem by digitally removing foliage from its virtual reconstruction while preserving the underlying branches and fruit. During testing, it produced fruit counts within 2% to 3% of the true number, compared with errors of up to 23% that can occur with conventional manual sampling methods. According to the University of Canterbury research team, the system can also calculate each fruit’s size, volume and surface area while tracking how individual fruit grow over time. Growers must decide weeks or months in advance how many seasonal workers to hire, how much packaging to order, how much cold storage will be needed and when fruit should be harvested. A poor estimate can leave farms scrambling for labour or paying for resources they never use.The UC Vision team has built mobile camera systems that move along vineyard rows and orchard lanes, capturing plants from multiple angles. One version scans vineyards through dense grape canopies, while another taller system maps orchard trees up to about 3.5 metres (11.5 feet) high. The resulting 3D models give growers detailed information about each individual fruit rather than broad estimates based on samples. Researchers say that level of precision could reduce waste throughout the production chain while improving planning across large commercial operations. The work has already been tested across 20 commercial farms, helping researchers refine the technology under real growing conditions rather than controlled laboratory settings. According to the University of Canterbury, those large-scale field trials are intended to ensure the system performs reliably before commercial rollout. Because the AI identifies individual fruit and links them to specific branches, future robotic systems could make decisions that today’s harvesting machines cannot. A robot could return several times during the season, picking only fruit that has reached the most valuable size while leaving smaller fruit to continue growing.The researchers point to cherries as one example. A difference of only a few millimetres in diameter can significantly increase market value, making selective harvesting economically attractive. Rather than stripping an entire tree in one pass, an autonomous machine could identify ripe cherries individually and revisit the orchard later for the remainder of the crop. Similar systems could eventually assist with pruning, thinning and precision spraying, reducing unnecessary work while improving productivity.The team is now preparing the technology for commercial deployment through a venture called HoloCrop, which aims to bring precision horticulture tools to growers. While fully autonomous orchards are still some distance away, researchers believe creating accurate digital twins of plants is a necessary first step. For an industry where leaves have long hidden crucial information from both farmers and machines, teaching AI to look beyond the foliage could prove just as valuable as teaching robots how to harvest the fruit itself.
Article Summary: Researchers in New Zealand have developed an artificial intelligence system that can digitally ‘see through’ dense foliage. The technology could help growers estimate harvests far more accurately, reduce waste and eventually allow robots to prune, spray and even pick fruit based on its size and maturity.

Article Title: Google DeepMind VP makes an important 'clarification' on science team: The culture of Google DeepMind is to...
Article Text:
FILE - Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai speaks about Google DeepMind at a Google I/O event in Mountain View, Calif., Wednesday, May 10, 2023. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File)

What the report said about DeepMind's AlphaFold team and its research strategy shift

Why John Jumper's move to Anthropic makes the timing of the clarification awkward for Google

Google DeepMind's vice-president of research, Pushmeet Kohli, has publicly pushed back on the idea that the company has quietly walked away from scientific research. Writing on X, Kohli said the DeepMind Science team has not pivoted at all. It has expanded its work, he said, and is still going after the hardest problems in science and biology.The clarification did not come out of nowhere. It follows a Financial Times report that said DeepMind has broken up the team behind AlphaFold, the protein-structure prediction system that won John Jumper and Demis Hassabis the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. According to the FT, most of the original AlphaFold paper authors have been moved to other projects over the past year, many of them onto work built around Gemini. Nearly a quarter of the full-time Google DeepMind authors on those papers have left the company entirely.Kohli's post reads like a direct rebuttal to that framing. He listed what the team is still working on: understanding protein function, decoding the genome, de-novo protein and enzyme design, plus Gemini-powered agents meant to speed up the research process itself. Then came the line that carried the most weight. The culture at Google DeepMind, he said, is to empower its scientists, who have agency over which hard goals they choose to chase.That applied to the AlphaFold team too.The FT's account describes a lab reorganising around large language models. Researchers who once sat on a single grand challenge have been scattered across enzyme design, nuclear fusion and genomics, with others moving to Alphabet's drug discovery arm Isomorphic Labs, which was spun out in 2021 and now works with Novartis and Eli Lilly. Kohli himself told the paper the strategy has evolved, with DeepMind now building Gemini systems that assist scientists and eventually automate parts of the scientific method.The detail that stings is the talent flow. Jumper and fellow AlphaFold researcher Jonas Adler were pulled onto Google's internal "Code Strike" team earlier this year, a group set up to close the gap with Anthropic and OpenAI on AI coding. Last month Jumper said he was leaving for Anthropic. Adler and AlphaFold colleague Alexander Pritzel are going with him.That is a Nobel laureate and two core collaborators walking out of a lab that built its identity on long-horizon science. Kohli's argument is that scientists choosing their own problems is a feature, not a failure. Critics reading the same facts see a research lab reshaped by a chatbot race it is trying to win.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind's vice-president of research Pushmeet Kohli has publicly pushed back on the idea that the company has quietly walked away from scientific research. Kohli said the DeepMind Science team has not pivoted at all. It has expanded its work, he said, and is still going after the hardest problems in science and biology.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda Gates, ‘There are all kinds of people and things that will come into your life, and if you can be flexible and adaptable, change doesn’t have to be scary’
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Melinda Gates



What Melinda Gates' quote means



A message reflected in her work



A simple takeaway



Melinda Gates has lived through more reinvention than most people experience in several lifetimes. From her early years at Microsoft to co-leading one of the world's largest philanthropic foundations, to more recently redefining her identity and work outside a decades-long partnership and marriage, her life has been a continuous negotiation with change. When she speaks about flexibility, she is not repeating a comforting cliché. She is describing a survival skill she has had to practise repeatedly, often in full public view."There are all kinds of people and things that will come into your life, and if you can be flexible and adaptable, change doesn't have to be scary."The quote begins with an observation rather than an instruction: life will bring "all kinds of people and things" into your path, many of them unplanned and some of them unwelcome. Gates is not suggesting that we get to choose what arrives. What we do get to choose, in her framing, is the posture we take toward it. That distinction is the entire argument of the quote.Most people experience change as something that happens to them, a force acting from the outside. Gates reframes it as something that happens with them, provided they are willing to bend rather than resist. The word "if" carries real weight here.She is not promising that change becomes painless. She is saying that flexibility is the condition under which fear loses its grip. Without adaptability, change remains frightening by default. With it, the same change becomes something closer to navigable.There is also an implicit critique of rigidity in the quote. The more fixed a person's expectations are about how life should unfold, the more that person will suffer when reality diverges from the plan. Adaptability, by contrast, is not the absence of preference or direction. It is the willingness to hold plans loosely enough that they can be revised without the revision feeling like failure.Melinda Gates's own career offers a working example of this idea in practice. She moved from a technical role at Microsoft into philanthropic leadership, a shift that required learning entirely new domains — global health, agricultural development, gender equity — largely in public and often without a roadmap. Building the Gates Foundation alongside Bill Gates meant absorbing new information constantly, adjusting strategy as programmes succeeded or failed, and working across cultures and communities very different from her own.Perhaps most visibly, her decision to leave the foundation and establish Pivotal Ventures, and to rebuild her personal and professional life independently in her sixties, was itself an act of adaptability at a scale most people never have to attempt. She has spoken about needing to relearn who she was outside a partnership that had defined her public identity for decades. That kind of change does not happen because someone chooses to be unafraid. It happens because someone chooses to be flexible enough to keep moving despite the fear.The quote works best as a practical filter rather than a piece of inspiration to admire from a distance. The next time an unexpected person enters your life, a plan falls apart, or circumstances shift in a direction you did not choose, the relevant question is not "How do I stop this from happening?" It is "How adaptable am I willing to be in response?" Gates is not asking anyone to welcome disruption with enthusiasm. She is pointing out that rigidity is what makes change feel unbearable, while flexibility is what makes it survivable — and sometimes, eventually, worthwhile.
Article Summary: Melinda Gates has lived through more reinvention than most people experience in several lifetimes. From early years at Microsoft to co-leading one of the world's largest philanthropic foundations, her life has been a continuous negotiation with change. When she speaks about flexibility, she is not repeating a comforting cliché. She is describing a survival skill she has had to practise repeatedly.

Article Title: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani filed motion to ban delivery app Motoclick, now he is going after Uber Eats and DoorDash; accuses apps of hiding tip buttons and set default...
Article Text:
Mamdani says NYC forced Uber Eats and DoorDash to unhide tip buttons, putting $104 million back in delivery workers' pockets since January.

What actually changed on January 26 for food delivery apps in the NYC, and why the tip button sits at checkout now

From Motoclick to the giants: how the NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration escalated its delivery app fight

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani opened his term by trying to shut a delivery app down. Six months later, he has the two biggest names in the business in his sights. On Wednesday, Mamdani said the city's crackdown on hidden tip buttons at Uber Eats and DoorDash has pushed an extra $104 million into delivery workers' pockets since January, and signalled the enforcement drive is far from over."Uber Eats and DoorDash hid tip buttons and set default tips below 10%. As a result, tips for delivery workers fell 79%," the mayor posted on X, saying the city forced the platforms to redesign their apps in January. He called the result the start of a longer push on how the apps treat the people working on them.The figures come from a Department of Consumer and Worker Protection report released alongside him. In the four weeks before the rules kicked in, workers averaged $1.18 in tips per delivery. In the four weeks after, that rose to $2.29. The city's roughly 70,000 app-based delivery workers are now on pace to earn an extra $184 million a year, about $2,287 each.Since that date, apps operating in the city must show customers a clear tipping option before payment: a selectable 10% tip, a custom amount, or nothing at all. The rule exists because of what happened the last time the city acted. When the minimum pay standard for delivery workers took effect in December 2023, Uber Eats and DoorDash buried their tipping menus, a move DCWP estimates cost workers around $550 million.The industry's warning that tipping rules would dent orders hasn't shown up in the data. Weekly orders are running at 3.3 million, about 700,000 higher than in December 2023. Hourly earnings including tips have climbed from $10.48 to $27.32, a 161% jump.The first target was smaller. In January, the city sued Motoclick and its CEO, seeking to shut the operation down, accusing it of charging workers $10 penalties on cancelled orders and deducting the full cost of refunded meals from their pay.Enforcement has since widened. Mamdani pointed to a January settlement requiring Uber Eats and other platforms to pay more than $5 million, and said DCWP's budget grew by over $4 million in June to add staff. The tipping law survived a legal challenge from both companies. Neither responded to requests for comment.
Article Summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani says crackdown on tip buttons at Uber Eats and DoorDash has pushed an extra $104 million into delivery workers' pockets since January. In January, apps operating in the city must show customers a clear tipping option before payment: a selectable 10% tip, a custom amount, or nothing at all.

Article Title: US Environmental Protection Agency expands Ratepayer Protection Pledge that Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and hundreds of other companies have signed; making a promise on electricity bills t
Article Text:
Representative Image

"build, bring, or buy all of the energy needed to power their facilities and to pay the full cost of that energy and its supporting infrastructure, no matter what."

EPA links pledge to AI infrastructure expansion

"islanded"

“Ensuring that the United States maintains our artificial intelligence dominance is essential to national security and economic prosperity. At the same time, it is equally important that we safeguard our communities from

utility price hikes

. This guidance will provide an avenue to do both. EPA is proud to further the President’s agenda through commonsense approaches to regulating.”

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has expanded US President Donald Trump 's Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and hundreds of other tech companies have signed this pledge, committing to build, bring or buy all the energy needed to power their facilities and pay the full cost of that energy and its supporting infrastructure instead of passing those costs on to American households through higher electricity bills.The expanded pledge extends those obligations across electric utilities, developers and state regulators whose decisions affect what consumers pay each month. At the same time, the EPA issued guidance clarifying that certain power plants built exclusively for data centres and not connected to the public electricity grid are not subject to the Clean Air Act's Acid Rain Program, saying the move will support AI infrastructure development while reducing pressure on regional electricity grids.The EPA said companies signing the pledge are committing toAccording to the agency, the expanded pledge is intended to ensure that the costs of powering new AI infrastructure are borne by developers, utilities and regulators rather than residential customers.Alongside the expanded pledge, the EPA issued guidance stating thatpower generation facilities that are not connected to the public electricity grid are not covered by the Clean Air Act's Acid Rain Program. The agency said this interpretation gives developers greater flexibility in where and how quickly they can build new data centres while helping reduce strain on regional power grids.EPA Assistant Administrator for Air and Radiation Aaron Szabo said,The EPA's memorandum states that the Acid Rain Program generally applies to facilities that sell electricity or are required to report as generating units to the US Department of Energy. As “islanded” power generation facilities neither sell electricity to the public nor fall under those reporting requirements, the agency concluded they are not subject to the program. Meanwhile, it added that if such a facility later connects to the public grid, it may become subject to the Acid Rain Program's requirements.
Article Summary: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has expanded US President Donald Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and hundreds of other tech companies have signed this pledge, committing to build, bring or buy all of the energy needed to power their facilities.

Article Title: India’s Big Four: A global journey, an Indian Dream
Article Text:
Divakar Vijayasarathy

, CEO,

DVS Advisory Group

For years, India has aspired to build its own Big Four. The ambition has been echoed across industry and policy circles, reflecting the country's growing confidence in its professional services ecosystem. With one of the world's largest talent pools and a rapidly expanding economy, India undoubtedly has the capability to create globally respected professional services institutions.Yet, there is an important question that deserves closer attention: can India's Big Four truly be built by focusing only on India?The answer may lie beyond India's borders not because India lacks talent, but because the dynamics of the professional services industry have fundamentally changed. India has consistently produced world-class accountants, consultants, tax professionals and business advisors who are trusted by organisations across the globe. The challenge is no longer one of capability. It is one of structure.Professional Services Has Become an Infrastructure BusinessProfessional services is no longer driven solely by expertise and human capital. Today, competitive advantage is increasingly shaped by investments in artificial intelligence, technology platforms, cybersecurity, knowledge management, leadership development, branding, research and acquisitions.Firms that lead the industry are those that continuously invest in building capabilities that go well beyond traditional advisory services.Most Indian professional services firms continue to operate as partnerships. While this model has enabled steady growth over the years, it also limits access to long-term capital. Growth is largely funded through retained earnings, making it difficult to invest at the same scale as globally integrated firms. Consequently, both revenues and investments remain predominantly domestic, creating structural limitations that become more evident as firms seek to compete internationally.Bigger Firms Alone Will Not Create India's Big FourMuch of the current industry conversation revolves around consolidation. Mergers between Indian firms can certainly create larger organisations with broader capabilities and greater operational efficiencies. However, scale alone is unlikely to create India's equivalent of the global Big Four.Consolidation may create India's largest accounting firm, but it does not fundamentally alter the business model. Revenues continue to be generated in the same market. Pricing remains linked to domestic economic realities. Capital constraints persist, and regulatory limitations continue to shape the industry. Simply put, scale without changing the source of value creation creates a larger version of the same institution rather than a globally competitive one.The Real Differentiator Is Client OwnershipOne of the defining strengths of the world's leading professional services firms lies not merely in the quality of their people but in where they build client relationships and where they generate value.A domestic Indian accounting firm may generate annual revenues of approximately ₹25–30 lakh per professional, while firms operating in developed markets often generate 5x–10x higher revenues per employee. The difference is not simply a matter of productivity. It reflects the markets where strategic advice is delivered, where long-term client relationships are established and where business value is ultimately priced.Global firms own the client relationship. They originate mandates, advise on strategic decisions, lead complex transactions and deliver integrated solutions by leveraging capabilities across multiple geographies. Their revenues are global, their investment capacity is global and, consequently, their ability to innovate is also global.This is the structural advantage that Indian firms must seek to build.The Next Chapter Is About Creating Value, Not Just Delivering ItIndia has already established itself as one of the world's most trusted execution hubs. Its professionals support businesses across industries and geographies, delivering high-quality work at scale. That achievement has positioned India as an indispensable part of the global professional services ecosystem. However, the next phase of growth requires a shift in focus.The future belongs to firms that own the client relationship, shape business strategy, originate transactions, develop intellectual property and orchestrate integrated global solutions not merely execute work on behalf of others.The objective should not be to become a lower-cost destination for professional services. It should be to become a creator of higher-value advisory institutions that influence strategic decision-making across markets. Lower costs create vendors. Ownership creates institutions.Building Globally Relevant PlatformsThe opportunity before Indian firms extends far beyond the domestic market. They can become trusted advisors helping multinational corporations invest in India, supporting Indian enterprises expanding overseas, facilitating cross-border transactions and connecting global investors with India's growth story.Achieving this ambition requires more than geographic expansion. It demands multidisciplinary capabilities that integrate tax, transactions, technology, legal, compliance, capital markets, artificial intelligence, managed services and strategic advisory into a seamless client experience.Equally important is the creation of proprietary products, digital platforms and intellectual property rooted in India's entrepreneurial strengths. Competing solely on cost is no longer sufficient. Sustainable differentiation will increasingly come from innovation, specialised expertise and the ability to solve complex global business challenges.Diversification Will Define the Next GenerationAnother important lesson comes from the evolution of the global professional services industry itself. The world's leading firms no longer rely solely on audit or tax services. They have built integrated businesses spanning consulting, digital transformation, cybersecurity, technology implementation, transactions and industry-specific advisory.A useful analogy is that of two movie theatres. One earns revenue only from ticket sales, while the other generates income from food and beverages, premium experiences, memberships and advertising. The difference in profitability is driven not by ticket sales alone, but by the breadth of its offerings. Professional services follows the same principle. Firms with broader capabilities create stronger client relationships, generate higher-value engagements and build more resilient businesses over time.Looking Beyond India's BordersIndia does not simply need another large accounting firm. It needs globally integrated professional services institutions capable of competing with the world's best. Building such institutions will require Indian firms to establish client-facing capabilities in developed markets, own international revenue streams, strengthen multidisciplinary expertise and build enduring relationships across major financial centres. When revenues are earned globally while leveraging India's exceptional talent and execution capabilities, stronger economics naturally follow. However, stronger economics should be viewed as the outcome—not the strategy.The larger objective is to transform India from being recognised primarily as the world's execution engine into one of the world's foremost creators of globally respected professional services platforms.The aspiration to build India's own Big Four remains both relevant and achievable. But paradoxically, that journey is unlikely to begin by expanding across Indian cities alone. It will begin by owning client relationships across New York, London, Singapore, Dubai, Sydney, Frankfurt and other global financial centres while leveraging India's extraordinary talent, innovation and entrepreneurial energy to create value for businesses around the world. That is why the road to India's Big Four may, paradoxically, begin outside India.
Article Summary: India has consistently produced world-class accountants, consultants, tax professionals and business advisors who are trusted by organisations across the globe. The challenge is no longer one of capability. It is one of structure. Most Indian professional services firms continue to operate as partnerships.

Article Title: Americans take note, FCC's new 'Chinese robot ban' also includes these vacuum cleaners
Article Text:
FCC's robot ban isn't just about humanoids—your next robot vacuum is caught in it too

Why a Roomba counts as an 'advanced robotic device' under the FCC's new rules

Chinese brands dominate robot vacuums , and the waiver route is nearly impossible

When the Trump administration announced this week that it was blocking "advanced robotic devices" from entering the United States, the coverage went straight to humanoids and robot dogs. The FCC chair even tweeted an image of them. But the fine print in the National Security Determination, dated July 27, covers a machine far more likely to be sitting in an American living room right now: the robot vacuum.FCC media relations director Katie Gorscak confirmed to The Verge that robovacs fall under the ban. Nobody is confiscating your Roomba, and companies can keep importing and selling models that already have approval. Future ones are the problem. And since almost every robot vacuum on the market is designed or built outside the US, "future ones" effectively means most of them.The definition is what does the damage. A device qualifies if it moves across the ground, weighs over 4.4 pounds including its dock, carries a sensor that perceives its surroundings, connects to a network at 200 kbps or better, and runs software that handles navigation.That is a robot vacuum described almost to the spec sheet. It also catches robot lawnmowers, sidewalk delivery bots and the warehouse robots shuttling packages around Amazon fulfilment centres.The exemption list is specific: self-driving cars, trains, drones, underwater vehicles, surgical robots, wheelchairs and fixed industrial arms. Cleaning robots did not make the cut, which is arguably consistent. The government's own determination cites a 2026 vulnerability that let someone remotely reach thousands of home robots worldwide, complete with camera feeds, microphone audio and floor maps.Here is where the market maths gets ugly. The top five robovac makers by share are Roborock, Ecovacs, Dreame, Xiaomi and Narwal. All Chinese. The Roomba brand itself, after iRobot's bankruptcy, is now owned by Picea, its former Chinese contract manufacturer. Dyson has been leaning on Chinese production too. IDC analyst Jitesh Ubrani told The Verge that non-Chinese brands are so few and so small that tracking their share is difficult.Foreign producers can apply for conditional approval, but the price of entry is a commitment to onshore manufacturing. American firms are not automatically safe either. Matic, assembled in California, may still need a waiver for new models because it does not source 65 percent of components domestically, co-founder Mehul Nariyawala said.Notably, the FCC is not asking applicants a single question about security practices. The waiver form wants to know where a robot is designed, made, assembled and tested. Reuters reported, citing four sources, that many non-Chinese suppliers are expected to be exempted anyway.The pattern echoes March's wireless router ban and the earlier drone restrictions. Engadget notes foreign-made power inverters are caught up in the same order, which could complicate life for accessory brands like Anker. For US buyers, the near-term effect is simple: whatever robovac is on shelves now may be the last of its kind for a while.
Article Summary: Chinese brands dominate robot vacuums, and the waiver route is nearly impossible. It also catches robot lawnmowers, sidewalk delivery bots and the warehouse robots shuttling packages around Amazon fulfilment centres. The FCC is not asking applicants a single question about security practices.

Article Title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella confirms Copilot super app, says 'Copilot is evolving rapidly'
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Staya Nadella

Microsoft Copilot usage continues to grow



Microsoft is not alone in building super apps



Microsoft is preparing to launch a new Copilot super app, CEO Satya Nadella announced during the company’s second quarter earnings call. The app will bring together the company’s AI chatbot, coding assistant, coworking tools and autonomous AI agents into a single platform for both consumers and businesses. Announcing the super app, Satya Nadella said that Copilot is evolving beyond a chatbot into a broader AI assistant. "Copilot is evolving rapidly from chat to Cowork to autopilots," Nadella said. "And this quarter, we are bringing these Copilot experiences together, including Code, in one super app spanning both consumer and commercial experiences. This is a major step forward, and I look forward to sharing more soon," he further added.According to earlier reports, the app will allow users to switch between personal and enterprise versions of Copilot while bringing together AI chat, coding, workplace collaboration and AI agents under one interface.During its second quarter earnings call, Microsoft also highlighted strong user growth for Copilot. "The number of conversations per user nearly doubled year over year," Nadella said.He added that "Average weekly engagement is on par with Outlook and Teams," while the time needed for customers to reach high monthly usage has fallen "from months to just days over the past year."Microsoft reported stronger-than-expected quarterly revenue, driven by continued growth in its cloud business. The company also announced a change in the estimated useful life of its data centres and office buildings, extending it from 15 years to 25 years.Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the accounting change means future data centre leases will be treated as operating leases rather than finance leases, reducing the amount that counts towards the company's reported capital expenditure going forward.Microsoft's announcement comes as AI companies increasingly shift towards "super apps" that combine multiple AI tools in one product. Sam Altman-led OpenAI has also been working towards a broader ChatGPT experience. According to recent reports, the company is preparing one of ChatGPT's biggest updates since launch. Anthropic has already combined its Claude chatbot with Claude Cowork.Companies such as X (formerly Twitter), Uber and Airbnb have also expressed ambitions to build all-in-one digital platforms.
Article Summary: Microsoft is preparing to launch a new Copilot super app, CEO Satya Nadella announced. The app will bring together the company’s AI chatbot, coding assistant, coworking tools and autonomous AI agents into a single platform for both consumers and businesses. Microsoft also highlighted strong user growth for Copilot.

Article Title: Europe’s Big 4 can't stop making embarrassing AI mistakes, PWC's Thought Leadership report 'forgets' ChatGPT cannot be a 'Source'
Article Text:
Big Four accounting form PwC has come under fire for a reports that allegedly contains AI “hallucinations”.

the URL for a cybersecurity report included the tracking tag utm_source=chatgpt.com

PwC Middle East said it “takes the accuracy of our published research seriously and is updating a limited number of supporting citations”

The Big Four’s ‘AI struggles’ in reports



In June, KPMG pulled its global report on “Agentic Al”

In May, Financial Times reported that EY Canada had to remove a report on loyalty rewards programmes

In November, Deloitte landed in trouble for the second time in a month

Big Four accounting and consulting giant PwC has come under fire after an investigation revealed that several of its middle eastern “thought leadership” reports contained AI-generated “hallucinations,” fabricated footnotes and chatbot citations, including a reference that listed ChatGPT directly in its source URL. The findings, uncovered by researchers at AI-detection platform GPTZero and verified by the Financial Times, highlight struggles among top consulting firms as they attempt to market AI advisory services while using generative tools to write their own research.The investigation flagged four PwC Middle East reports published over the past two years. The documents covered topics such as corporate strategy for “agentic” AI bots, government public service guides, and market forecasts for electric vehicles in the region.According to the report by the Financial Times, researchers found that a significant portion of the citations in the reports were flawed. For example, one report cited a study on air quality in Riyadh that appears to be completely hallucinated by AI as there is no trace of the paper exists in the referenced journal or under the listed authors.In a second incident, multiple footnotes linked to broken web pages or articles that contained no mention of the claims they were supposed to support.Thirdly, to support a “real-world success story” about a JPMorgan AI initiative, PwC cited a teenage blogger on Medium with just 280 followers. The actual initiative took place in 2017—five years before ChatGPT was launched.Moreover, a single claim regarding traffic accidents was repeated three times across two pages, with each instance featuring entirely different citations. In one glaring footnote,, effectively revealing that the source material was surfaced directly through a ChatGPT prompt.In a statement to the publication,across the flagged reports.PwC is not the only member of the “Big Four” to face public embarrassment over unverified AI content. Previous investigations by GPTZero led rivals EY and KPMG to retract published research papers after similar hallucinations were uncovered.after major companies and organisations named in it complained that their supposed achievements were completely made up. The professional services giant published the report, titled "Redefining excellence in the age of agentic Al," with numerous false claims and bogus case studies, according to a report by The Financial Times.from its website after researchers identified several mistakes. The report, which was allegedly Al-generated, apparently included Al hallucinations, inaccurate citations and references to studies that do not exist. The consulting firm said it was "reviewing the circumstances that led to this article's publication" following scrutiny over the report.after it prepared a major healthcare report for the Canadian government. As reported by The Independent, the report, which was supposed to assess healthcare services in Newfoundland and Labrador, contained multiple factual errors that are believed to be generated by artificial intelligence tools.
Article Summary: Big Four accounting and consulting giant PwC has come under fire after an investigation revealed that several of its middle eastern “thought leadership” reports contained AI-generated “hallucinations,” fabricated footnotes and chatbot citations. The findings, uncovered by researchers at AI-detection platform GPTZero and verified by the Financial Times, highlight struggles among top consulting firms.

Article Title: US Senator introduces bill he calls 'commonsense fix to America's outdated immigration system', says: Immigrants should be able to call America home if they ...
Article Text:
US Senator Alex Padilla announces bill to reopen lawful pathway to legalization

Us bill proposes new pathway to green cards



US Senator Alex Padilla calls proposal a 'commonsense fix'

US Senator Alex Padilla has introduced a bill aimed at expanding a pathway to lawful permanent residency for millions of long-term immigrants, calling it a "commonsense fix" to America's immigration system. Announcing the legislation in Los Angeles, Padilla said immigrants who have lived in the United States continuously for at least seven years, paid taxes, contributed to their communities and have no criminal record should have an opportunity to obtain a green card. “It’s common sense that immigrants who pose no safety threat and contribute to our country should be able to call America home with certainty” said US Senate Democratic Whip Durbin, Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee.The proposal would update a decades-old provision of U.S. immigration law that has not been revised since 1986, replacing the current eligibility cutoff date with a rolling seven-year requirement. Alex Padilla's Renewing Immigration Provisions of the Immigration Act of 1929 would amend the Registry provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act.Under the proposal, immigrants would be eligible to apply for lawful permanent resident status if they have continuously lived in the U.S.for at least seven years before applying, have no criminal record, and meet all other existing eligibility requirements for a green card.The bill would also replace the fixed eligibility date with a rolling cutoff, removing the need for Congress to update the law periodically.Padilla said the legislation would provide a pathway to legal permanent residency for more than 8 million people, including Dreamers, Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders, children of long-term visa holders, essential workers and some highly skilled workers waiting for employment-based green cards."We believe that if you've lived here for over seven years, paid taxes for years, contributed to your community for years, and you don't have a criminal record, then you deserve a pathway to legalization," Padilla said.He added, "My bill is a commonsense fix to our outdated immigration system" and said it would update an existing legal pathway rather than create a new government programme.
Article Summary: US Senator Alex Padilla has introduced a bill aimed at expanding a pathway to lawful permanent residency for millions of long-term immigrants. The proposal would update a decades-old provision of U.S. immigration law that has not been revised since 1986. Padilla said immigrants who have lived in the United States continuously for at least seven years and have no criminal record should have an opportunity to obtain a green card.

Article Title: China responds to US bans on Chinese robots and power inverters; tells what Europe too has been saying: Stop threatening our companies with ...
Article Text:
Representative image

What US government said on banning China’s humanoid robots

China’s response to US bans on Chinese robots

FCC’s aggressive stance

Echoes of Europe’s concerns

The Trump administration has expanded the FCC Covered List to include advanced robotic devices and connected power inverters, effectively banning imports from new Chinese-made humanoid and Microsoft CFO's internal memo tells employees that its biggest AI bets are paying off. The move comes as the US government continues to tighten its control on Chinese technology across sectors ranging from telecommunications and drones to artificial intelligence to now humanoid robots. Notably, Elon Musk has previously described China’s humanoid robots as Tesla’s biggest long-term competition. The FCC said these devices pose “unacceptable risks” to US national security, citing vulnerabilities that could allow foreign actors to surveil Americans or disrupt the power grid.In its determination of the threats posed by robots, FCC said: “As the technology matures, advanced robotic devices have growing use cases in monitoring and securing critical infrastructure. Robots are often equipped with high-fidelity sensors, including Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), tactile, acoustic, and thermal sensors that collect and maintain sensitive data on their surroundings”.“In addition to securing critical infrastructure, advanced robotic devices also have applications in industrial manufacturing, from material handling to order fulfilment.Integrating these technologies into American manufacturing will lower production costs, increase output, and support America’s reindustrialization. In order for the American economy to rely on these technologies, we must have a secure domestic advanced robotics supply chain and industrial Base,” it further stated.Adding further, the FCC said, “All foreign-produced advanced robotic devices pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States and to the safety and security of U.S. persons and should be included on the FCC’s Covered List, unless the Department of War (DOW) transmits to the FCC a specific determination that a given foreign-produced advanced robotic device, or a class of such devices, does not pose such risks”.According to a report by South China Morning Post report, the Chinese embassy in Washington condemned the move, urging the U.S. to “abandon its hegemonic mindset” and stop threatening Chinese companies with sanctions. Embassy spokesman Liu Chang told the South China Morning Post that Beijing opposes the politicisation of science, technology, and trade issues, calling the bans “groundless pretexts.” He warned that China would take “all necessary measures” to safeguard its interests.The report further adds, under chairman Brendan Carr, the FCC has become one of Washington’s most aggressive regulators targeting Chinese tech firms. Recent actions include bans on Chinese drones, restrictions on foreign-made routers, and moves to evict Chinese telecom carriers from U.S. networks. Republican Senator Jim Banks welcomed the latest decision, saying advanced robotics and inverters are “essential to re-industrialisation and critical infrastructure. ”China’s statement echoed what European regulators have also been saying: stop threatening companies with sanctions and avoid turning technology competition into geopolitical confrontation. European officials have repeatedly cautioned Washington against unilateral bans that could fragment global supply chains.
Article Summary: The FCC has expanded its Covered List to include advanced robotic devices and connected power inverters. The move effectively bans imports from new Chinese- made humanoid robots. The FCC said these devices pose ‘unacceptable risks’ to US national security.

Claude users see '529 Overloaded' error
