We're working to recover Opus 5 as well."Earlier, Anthropic had said it had identified the issue and was working on a fix.During the outage, users attempting to access Claude or applications powered by Anthropic's API encountered error messages.One of the most common messages displayed was: "API Error: 529 Overloaded. This is a server-side issue, usually temporary — try again in a moment." A 529 Overloaded error generally indicates that servers are unable to handle the current volume of incoming requests.The disruption affected not only the Claude chatbot but also third-party tools and services that depend on Anthropic's API. Users reported failed requests, higher latency and interrupted AI responses while the incident was ongoing.Anthropic said it has already seen recovery across most Claude models but warned that some users may continue to experience errors until the issue is fully resolved.

Article Title: When Steve Jobs told Oracle founder Larry Ellison: You don't need more money, so do not ...
Article Text:
Oracle founder Larry Ellison

When Larry Ellison wanted to buy Apple

'The most expensive real estate on earth'

Larry Ellison recalled how Steve Jobs rejected his plan to buy Apple in the 1990s, telling him that making more money was not the goal. Speaking at the University of Southern California's 2016 commencement ceremony, Oracle founder Larry Ellison said he had arranged financing to acquire Apple, which was then valued at about $5 billion. But Apple founder Steve Jobs, who was no longer with the company after losing a bitter power struggle with CEO John Sculley and the company's board of directors, chose to return to Apple through its acquisition of NeXT. Jobs insisted that he wanted to lead the company from what he called the "moral high ground" rather than through a takeover that could benefit him financially.During his speech, Ellison said Apple was struggling at the time and his solution was straightforward. "My idea was simple. Buy Apple," he said. According to Ellison, Apple was worth around $5 billion then, and he had already arranged to borrow the money needed for the acquisition. "All Steve had to do was say yes," he recalled.Instead of selling Apple, Jobs proposed a different plan.Ellison said Jobs wanted Apple to acquire NeXT Computer, rejoin the company's board, and allow directors to decide on their own that he was the right person to lead Apple again.Wondering how the plan would benefit them financially, Ellison asked, "If we don't buy Apple, how are we going to make any money?"Steve Jobs' reply surprised him. "You don't need any more money," Jobs said.He added, "I'm not doing this for the money. I don't want to get paid. If I do this, I need to do this standing on the moral high ground."Larry Ellison said Steve Jobs' approach taught him an important lesson about leadership. He described the "moral high ground" as "the most expensive real estate on earth."According to Ellison, Jobs' decision ultimately paid off as he returned to Apple, rebuilt the company and turned it into "the most valuable company on earth."
Article Summary: Oracle founder Larry Ellison recalled how Steve Jobs rejected his plan to buy Apple in the 1990s. Ellison said he had arranged financing to acquire Apple, which was then valued at about $5 billion. Jobs insisted that he wanted to lead the company from what he called the "moral high ground"

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has a fresh challenge on his hands: Disney is dropping GitHub Copilot and several other AI coding tools in the US starting Augurs, according to an internal message viewed by Business Insider. This move of the company does not apply internationally, but it marks a significant setback for Microsoft’s AI product suite. Disney is now preparing to adopt OpenAI’s Codex as its coding assistant, while retaining access to Anthropic’s Claude Enterprise and Cursor. At the same time, Disney revealed that it will drop two Amazon tools which include the agentic code editor Kiro and AI assistant Q. Claude will also no longer be accessible through Amazon Web Services Bedrock.Eight Disney tech employees told Business Insider they rarely or never used GitHub Copilot. One product manager said Copilot produced “needlessly complex” code requiring clean-up, while a longtime engineer said their access had “lapsed for lack of use.” The frustration was compounded last month when Microsoft shifted Copilot’s pricing to a token-based model, sparking backlash even as executives claimed it fuelled GitHub’s “best month ever.Claude and Cursor have become fan favourites among Disney engineers. Some superusers reportedly invoke these tools tens of thousands of times per day, with one high-level engineer estimating that 80% of their coding at the terminal is done with Claude. Disney’s streaming leaders even created an AI adoption dashboard to track usage, encouraging staff to boost velocity and output.Microsoft has been working to revamp GitHub and shake up its Copilot teams to better compete with rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. But Disney’s decision underscores the uphill battle Nadella faces as Copilot struggles to gain traction in a market increasingly dominated by more popular AI coding assistants.Microsoft is spending a record $190 billion to build AI infrastructure, and it is still short enough on servers that it has started evaluating Amazon and Google—its two biggest cloud rivals—as suppliers.According to a Business Insider report, the company is now evaluating Amazon and Google as sources of additional cloud capacity, with one person familiar with the discussions putting it plainly: "We are shopping for capacity everywhere." Amazon has already stepped in once, bailing Microsoft out following a series of GitHub outages this year. Microsoft also explored leasing infrastructure from Oracle but walked away over security and compliance concerns. For a company whose Azure pitch rests on owning the stack end to end, that is an uncomfortable place to be.

Article Title: Less than a week after Thinking Machines cofounder Lilian Weng resigned citing stress and illness, she is rejoining Sam Altman
Article Text:
Health challenges among AI leaders



Less than a week after announcing her resignation from Thinking Machines Lab citing stress and illness, cofounder Lilian Weng is now returning to work alongside OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . According to a report by Business Insider, Weng, who previously served as OpenAI’s vice president of research and safety, said she had been ill more often in the past seven months than at any other point in her life. In her farewell post, she explained that the “consistent stress and workload” of building a startup had pushed her beyond what her health could sustain.Weng’s departure came as Thinking Machines was sprinting to release its first open-weight model, Inkling. She admitted feeling “guilt” about taking sick leave during that critical period and considered narrowing her role before deciding to step away entirely. “If I cannot give it 100% for what I should be responsible for, I fail my job,” she wrote. But just days later, Weng has chosen to rejoin Altman in a scoped role that promises more predictability and less strain than her cofounder responsibilities. A report by TechCrunch revealed that OpenAI has confirmed that Weng will be joining the company as the VP of AI Safety Research.“I've always been a curiosity-driven person. Leaning new knowledge or figuring out how to solve problems that are not well defined often gives me simple joy.The fun part of being a cofounder is how it "forced" me to develop new perspectives on company strategies, team building (at the company level), and much more, as well as how these seemingly abstract terms are deeply connected with our day-to-day actions, planning and narratives. With real-world experience, ideas that once felt theoretical become approachable and it is true for many terms in many domains,” wrote Weng in a post on X.Mira Murati the founder of Thinking Machines Lab thanked Weng for everything. “We’ll miss you, it’s been wonderful building Thinky together. I’m glad that you’re putting your health first. Thank you for everything.”Her move follows a string of health-related step-backs across the AI industry. Earlier this month, Fidji Simo left her full-time role as OpenAI’s CEO of AGI after a flare-up of POTS, while Greg Yang of xAI shifted into an advisory role after being diagnosed with Lyme disease. The pressures of leading frontier AI labs have increasingly highlighted the toll on executives’ health.Thinking Machines itself has been hit hard by Silicon Valley’s AI talent war. A Business Insider review found that 13 of its 42 founding members have left since launch, including three of its six cofounders, as rivals like Meta and OpenAI offered lucrative compensation packages. Weng’s return to Altman underscores how talent continues to circulate among the most influential players in AI.

One of 'biggest AI problems' is forcing American and European companies to use Chinese models



Canadian billionaire and former Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary feels that fear of China’s rise will be the driving force behind deeper economic integration between the United States, Canada and Mexico. O’Leary argued that each country brings unique strengths to the table: “Canada has the energy and critical minerals, the United States has the scale and innovation, and Mexico plays a vital role in the North American economy,” he said. He added that cooperation is not just good policy but “an economic necessity” as the race for AI, energy, and critical infrastructure accelerates.The comments made by the Canadian billionaire come amid the growing recognition of China’s technological momentum. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk also recently told Economist that China already produces far more electricity than the US and it could become the world’s AI leader if it manages to secure enough computing power.American AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic have also warned that Chinese rivals are closing the gap, with Beijing-based Moonshot AI drawing attention for its Kimi K3 model.Automobile executives including Ford CEO Jim Farley, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe, and Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi have repeatedly highlighted Chinese automakers’ dominance in electric vehicle production. Despite this, North America remains fragmented, with President Donald Trump recently imposing 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods.Recently, it was revealed that the cost of running sophisticated AI is pushing companies away from American labs toward China, a report has said, claiming that businesses ranging from Silicon Valley startups to European industrial giants are quietly replacing top-tier US AI models with cheaper Chinese alternatives, and integrating them into their business operations.A report by The Financial Times claims that household brands like DoorDash, Airbnb and German engineering giant Siemens have all adopted AI tools built in China. The mass migration is being fueled by a corporate race to solve the industry’s biggest headache: the ballooning cost of using AI caused by a sudden shift from flat-rate subscriptions to usage-based billing.Faced with massive bills, companies appear to have realised they no longer need the absolute most advanced and expensive model to handle everyday business routines. Article Title: Rogue AI agent of Sam Altman's OpenAI hacked more than one multi-billion company, a New York-based CTO makes new revelations
Article Text:
Sam Altman

Unauthenticated code exploited on Modal’s infrastructure



OpenAI confirms breach across multiple services



The rogue OpenAI agent that executed a high-profile cyberattack on world’s biggest AI model repository, Hugging Face, also acompromised a customer hosted by another technology company, Modal Labs. The new details, published by Hugging Face and reported by news agency Reuters, reveal that the experimental AI agent reached additional customer systems during its multi-day breakout earlier this month. In a blog post, Modal Labs clarified that "Modal's platform and isolation were not compromised in any way". Instead, "the environment involved was a customer's own application. It was deployed to a endpoint that was publicly accessible without authentication, and it was designed to compile and execute code submitted by anyone on the internet in a Modal Sandbox"."The code execution the attacker obtained took place inside that customer's own container, within Modal's standard sandbox isolation boundary. No other customer workloads were affected," the blog post stated.According to a timeline released by Hugging Face, the autonomous AI agent initially broke out of its sandbox, which is essentially an isolated testing space, hosted on a third-party provider’s infrastructure.The agent then used that breach as a launching pad for a broader platform-level attack on Hugging Face.Akshat Bubna, CTO of New York-based Modal Labs, confirmed that Modal was the third-party provider involved. However, Bubna emphasized that the breach stemmed from insecure code published by a customer, rather than a security flaw in Modal's core architecture.“Modal's platform or isolation were not compromised in any way,” Bubna told Reuters, explaining that the customer had “published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution”.While OpenAI declined to comment directly on Modal’s statements, the company pointed to an updated disclosure confirming that its agent accessed four accounts across four separate third-party services.OpenAI stated that while the agent accessed multiple accounts, it found “no other activity at the level of severity or scale of what we've shared related to Hugging Face, which involved a platform-level compromise”.
Article Summary: The rogue OpenAI agent that executed a high-profile cyberattack on world’s biggest AI model repository, Hugging Face, also acompromised a customer hosted by another technology company, Modal Labs. New details reveal that the experimental AI agent reached additional customer systems during its multi-day breakout earlier this month.

Article Title: Two solar farms in Minnesota restored native wildflowers and proved beneficial for bees, butterflies proving to scientists what everyone got wrong

How native vegetation helped pollinators recover

Why the findings matter

Solar farms and ecosystem restoration

Two solar farms in Minnesota have reportedly helped restore local ecosystems. According to a study by researchers at Argonne National Laboratory, the solar farms have restored native wildflowers and grasses while increasing populations of beneficial insects. The findings add what scientists describe as evidence that solar farms can contribute to habitat restoration and pollinator conservation when developed with native vegetation.After monitoring the two sites for five years, researchers found significant increases in native plants as well as in insects, including bees, butterflies, wasps, and hornets. Bee populations increased about 20-fold, while the overall number of beneficial insects tripled compared with earlier observations.The two solar farms were developed on retired agricultural land and replanted with native wildflowers and grasses. Researchers tracked changes in vegetation and insect populations over five years to assess how the sites affected local biodiversity.The study found that restoring native plant species created habitats that supported pollinating insects, with bees showing the largest increase. Butterflies, wasps and hornets also became more abundant as native vegetation became established.Researchers said the results are significant because expanding renewable energy infrastructure will require large areas of land. Estimates suggest that meeting future solar energy demand could require around 10 million acres for solar development.Using retired farmland and restoring it with native vegetation could reduce ecological impacts while creating habitats for pollinators. According to the researchers, insects supported by the solar farms also moved into nearby agricultural areas, where they helped pollinate crops.The findings come as insect populations continue to decline in many regions due to factors such as climate change and pesticide use. Beetles, bees, butterflies and other insects help pollinate crops and sustain healthy ecosystems. Other insects help sustain soil health and biodiversity.The Minnesota study shows that solar projects paired with native habitat restoration can not only generate renewable electricity, but also benefit local ecosystems and boost pollinator numbers.
Article Summary: Two solar farms in Minnesota have reportedly helped restore local ecosystems. Article Title: Quote of the Day by Julie Sweet: ‘I have an unwavering commitment to inclusion and diversity’
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Julie Sweet

Quote of the day by Accenture CEO Julie Sweet



"I have an unwavering commitment to

inclusion and diversity

."

What Julie Sweet's quote means

A message tested by real events



Julie Sweet has led Accenture, one of the world's largest professional services companies with roughly 770,000 employees across more than 120 countries, since 2019. A few themes have run through her public statements but one stands out and none of them is as consistently as this one. Unlike a lot of corporate language on the subject, which tends to stay vague and aspirational, Sweet has repeated this stance across interviews and reports for close to a decade. That repetition is itself part of the message: a position she keeps restating on the record.The word doing the heavy lifting here is “unwavering”. The quote adjusts a goal, a target and a program with a fixed personal position, framed as something that doesn't move regardless of business conditions, market pressure or the broader corporate climate. That's a stronger claim than most companies make about their own values, and it's also a harder one to walk back gracefully, which matters, given what's happened since.There’s also a shift worth noticing in how the sentence is built. Sweet says “I,” not “Accenture” or “we.” Most corporate diversity language is written to sound institutional and permanent. But Sweet's phrasing puts her own name behind it, tying her personal credibility to the outcome rather than hiding behind the company's.Sweet has used language like this publicly not long after taking over as CEO, and repeated it consistently through the years that followed, including in Accenture's Fiscal 2024 Annual Report, published in October 2024. Less than four months later, in February 2025, Sweet told employees in an internal memo that Accenture was ending several of its DEI-specific goals and programs, including its long-standing target of a gender-balanced global workforce by 2025 — a target the company had held since 2017.Around the same time, Accenture renamed its public-facing DEI webpage from “Our commitment to inclusion & diversity” to “Everyone is welcome here.” Accenture’s own framing of the shift was that the underlying commitment to a workplace where everyone belongs hadn't changed, even as the specific representation targets and named programs built around it were retired.Critics saw it differently, pointing to the gap between the language used just months earlier and the programs that were subsequently wound down. Either way, the episode is a real-world test of how durable a CEO's stated values turn out to be once external pressure – in this case, a broader US corporate retreat from DEI commitments through 2024 and 2025 – enters the picture.
Article Summary: Julie Sweet has led Accenture, one of the world's largest professional services companies, since 2019. The quote adjusts a goal, a target and a program with a fixed personal position. It's a stronger claim than most companies make about their own values.

Article Title: Apple’s incoming CEO John Ternus says company will expand entertainment business
Article Text:
Apple to focus on ‘quality over quantity’ strategy



Apple to leverage hardware and unique partnerships



Apple’s incoming CEO, hardware chief John Ternus, has committed to expanding the tech giant’s entertainment footprint when he officially takes the helm of the iPhone maker in September. Speaking on the red carpet at the fourth season premiere of “Ted Lasso” this week, Ternus highlighted the company's streaming trajectory alongside outgoing CEO Tim Cook, news agency Reuters reported.“I think we have such tremendous momentum right now in Apple TV. There's so many amazing shows, so many amazing characters and stories, and so we're just going to keep building on the momentum," Ternus told Reuters.Apple first launched its original TV series and films through Apple TV+ in 2019, securing major hits including the Oscar-winning film “CODA,” the box-office success “F1”, and acclaimed series such as “The Studio” and “Ted Lasso”. Last year, the company rebranded the service by dropping the ‘plus’ sign, renaming it simply Apple TV.Meanwhile, Cook noted that he is actively sharing insights about the entertainment industry as part of the leadership transition. Cook reiterated that Apple’s core strategy will remain focused on prestige content rather than volume.“Our role is to be the best. That's our lane. We're not about the most. There are...other companies that do that. But we're about the best, and I feel like we really hit our stride in providing that,” Cook explained.Cook highlighted that Apple remains open to future media partnerships, provided the company can bring unique technological innovations to the deal. He cited Apple’s broad partnership with Formula 1 as a prime model.Apple engineered custom camera systems for the Brad Pitt feature film “F1” to capture immersive racing footage while during the same time, F1 races started streaming exclusively on Apple TV in the US. Apple provides real-time leaderboards, updates and race coverage integrated directly into Apple News and companion apps.“We'll do things that we can bring something unique to, where we can innovate in a way that others might not be able to. I feel like we're really doing that with F1. We're so excited about how we're doing there and the viewership numbers that we're getting. So more things like that would be possible,” Cook said.The executive transition comes shortly after senior Apple executive Eddy Cue signaled that the company aims to deliver “better and more” films and TV shows across both streaming platforms and traditional cinemas in the coming years.
